item.title: I turned my Amazon Echo Dot into a Home Assistant voice satellite using a tool built with Claude
item.itunes:title: I turned my Amazon Echo Dot into a Home Assistant voice satellite using a tool built with Claude
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
An old Amazon Echo Dot 2nd gen is a surprisingly good listener. That little puck hears "Alexa" from across a room and over music, which is why old Echos are arguably the best Home Assistant voice hardware you can buy, as long as you never use Alexa again. Alexa was always the problem, not the hardware.

Plenty of people have replaced Alexa with a fully local voice assistant on new hardware, but I wanted to keep the Echo. A project called echo-dot-assist keeps the part that's genuinely good, and swaps out everything that talks to Amazon. Claude wrote its code in conversation with the project's author. I've already let Claude Code show me what my Home Assistant could actually do, so I'm cautiously in the first camp. It works, but I made two mistakes getting there, and the setup made one of its own.

I built an Amazon Echo killer with this ESP32-powered quad microphone array

It has four microphones and some great processing chops.

2
By  Adam Conway

What echo-dot-assist keeps, and what it throws out

Amazon's ears stay, Amazon's brain goes

The clever bit is what the project doesn't replace. Your Echo keeps Amazon's microphone processing and Amazon's own wake word engine, the same on-device detector a stock Echo runs. Only the Alexa client goes, replaced by a small daemon called hassmic that Home Assistant discovers as an ESPHome device. No YAML and no add-on, according to the project.

Then a firewall on the Echo itself keeps Amazon's programs on your local network. Some of Amazon's own services keep running for the audio side, but only hassmic may reach beyond your network, so it can fetch replies and music from wherever Home Assistant points it. Requests go to Home Assistant's Assist instead, and you get timers, announcements, a Bluetooth proxy, and its own settings page.

Claude wrote it, and the README says so up front

The disclosure is right at the top, and it's blunt. The project's README opens with a warning: "Vibecoded, unaudited, your risk." The author says Claude wrote the code, notes, and docs in conversation with them, and tested it on one Echo of each model.

That isn't me building anything with Claude, to be clear. It's someone else's AI-assisted project, and I'm the guy running it on hardware I don't mind losing. Sure, unaudited code that unlocks a bootloader is a big ask, but the honesty about it is refreshing, and the docs are upfront about what can go wrong.

You'll have to decide whether you trust the code enough to run it. After using it, the only thing that worries me is that any mistyped commands can brick your Echo Dot. That's no different from when I manually type the adb commands, and at least they're reproducible by using the script.

Only a handful of Echos can do this

Here's the catch, and it's a big one. Only certain models can be unlocked, and the model number on the bottom matters more than how the Echo looks. My first attempt stalled because I only owned an Echo Dot (3rd gen) and an Echo Dot (4th gen). The project lists the 4th gen as having no known exploit. The 3rd gen only works if it's the 2018 model, which means opening the case and connecting to test pads on the board, and its page warns that the unlock has left some recently updated units unusable.

The Echo Dot 2nd gen (RS03QR) is the easy one. It has a micro-USB port, so you don't need to open it or solder. Once I got my hands on one, the rest of the project took an hour.

Home Assistant doesn't just control smart devices, and that's where it gets interesting

The center of the home.

3
By  Rich Edmonds

The unlock is done by hand, and that's on purpose

R0rt1z2's exploit does the hard part, and he wants you to run it yourself

None of this would work without R0rt1z2, who built the exploits that unlock these MediaTek-based Echos and ported TWRP to them. Their XDA Forums thread for the Echo Dot 2 covers every file and step, and the echo-dot-assist setup sends you there instead of repeating them. That's deliberate, because R0rt1z2 asked that his unlocks be run only by hand, never from an installer or script.

So the setup waits while you do the scary part yourself. I used an Ubuntu-based box because the project says the unlock needs direct USB access, so no VM or WSL. Hold the Echo's action button while plugging it in, wait for a green ring, type YES, then leave it completely alone. When the ring turns white, TWRP is running, and the unlock is done.

The setup takes over once TWRP is up

From there, the setup script does almost everything. It wipes the Echo, flashes one specific Fire OS version into both of its system slots, pulls a signed build from GitHub so nothing compiles locally, locks down the network, joins your Wi-Fi, and installs the satellite. It shows a tidy 10-step checklist the whole way.

There's a dry-run mode, too, which prints every command without running any of them. It's also how I tripped myself up.

Your phone can run ADB on itself with no PC, and it's how I finally killed the bloatware I couldn't uninstall

Shizuku is a game-changer for tinkering lovers

2
By  Ayush Pande

It wasn't all smooth sailing

A dry run looks a lot like the real thing

The dry run walks all the way to a cheerful "is running" message at the end, so I assumed the firmware step was done. It wasn't, because a dry run runs nothing. I went ahead and installed boot-root, the root package from the XDA thread, and got this: (!) Error: boot cmdline has no veritykeyid

It ran before the setup flashed its firmware, and it stopped at the first step for the first slot. I ran the setup for real, let it flash both slots, and boot-root went through cleanly on the second try, patching both slots with no errors.

The setup gave up on a perfectly healthy Echo

After the install, the final check failed in red: "Checking it stays up." The check looks for the satellite twice, 10 seconds apart, and the second look came up empty. That looked like a crash loop, but the Echo's log showed hassmic reporting in about 131 seconds after boot, followed by "self test: passed." So I skipped the check, and it has worked fine since.

The firewall is the bit that actually matters

The log also shows the privacy promise in action. At boot, the Echo writes firewall rules that let its traffic reach private, link-local, multicast, and broadcast addresses, and drop everything else. The exceptions are DNS lookups and hassmic itself, which the project lets out so it can fetch replies and music. Boot-root also disables Amazon's update service, and the satellite's own online updates are off by default.

One fun detail: the Echo's log shows my network handed it Google's 8.8.8.8 as a second DNS server. The firewall deliberately allows DNS to whatever servers the network hands out, so Amazon's programs can still look up Amazon's addresses; they just can't connect to them. The project also notes the lock doesn't cover the few seconds between the Echo joining Wi-Fi at boot and the firewall going up, so the project suggests blocking the Echo at your router too, if "never" has to mean never. I haven't, so I'm calling it firewalled rather than airtight.

My smart TV's outbound traffic genuinely worried me, and now it has its own rules

It's not that I don't trust it (which I don't) but you shouldn't either

By  Joe Rice-Jones

Living with an Echo that answers to Home Assistant

It worked on the first command

Home Assistant discovered the Echo as a new ESPHome device on its own, and the first thing I said to it turned on my homelab plug. To be clear about where the speech goes: my Home Assistant setup uses Home Assistant Cloud for speech-to-text and text-to-speech, so audio of the request does leave my network, just not to Amazon. If you want it fully local, Home Assistant supports local speech engines too.

The settings page is where it gets fun. You can boost the speaker gain, turn the Echo into a Bluetooth speaker for your phone, use it as a Bluetooth proxy for Home Assistant, and even Drop In between Echos on your own network. Your browser signs every change, and you can log in with a press of the Echo's action button.

I'm sticking with Amazon's wake word engine

You can swap Amazon's engine for microWakeWord, the open engine ESPHome's satellites use, or let Home Assistant listen with openWakeWord. The project labels microWakeWord as experimental, and the Home Assistant option streams the Echo's microphone to your server constantly. Neither felt worth it when the stock engine is already this good at hearing me. I didn't time it with a stopwatch, but replies feel as quick as they did on a stock Dot.

There's also a "Download from Amazon" option for extra wake words like "Computer." It needs an Amazon sign-in, and the Echo shows up in your Alexa app until you sign it out. I skipped it, because the whole point was getting Amazon out of the loop.

ESPHome turned my junk drawer into a smart home

The set up has never been easier.

By  Jasmine Mannan

If you have the right Echo, this is a no-brainer

Amazon sold a lot of very capable microphones very cheaply, and this project keeps the best part of them while cutting the cord. My Echo Dot 2 now hears me like it always did, but it answers to my smart home instead of Amazon's.

It's not for everyone, though. The tool is unaudited by its own admission, and only a few models qualify, so flip your Echo over before you get excited. If yours doesn't make the cut, LocalDot is a replacement board for the 3rd-gen Echo Dot that's crowdfunding now, with shipping expected in 2027, and it covers the 2019 refresh too. Or you can always use the Home Assistant Voice Preview Edition if you'd rather not unlock anything at all. Self-hosting your voice assistant doesn't have to start with a bootloader exploit.

item.itunes:title: One device now controls my PC, home lab, Mac, and laptop at once
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If you've got a multi-system desk, then managing this setup can create substantial peripheral clutter and workflow friction. If you've got a primary Windows desktop, a Mac workstation, a laptop, and then a headless or rack-mounted home lab server, you might start to feel overwhelmed with all of the devices you need to control each of them.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Standard hardware KVM switches or software-based network KVMs solve the keyboard-sharing issue, but they still require a separate pointing device or rely on active network connections that can fail during BIOS configuration or OS recovery. By consolidating both typing and cursor input into a single compact chassis in the form of the Clevetura S, this addresses both physical desk footprint and cross-platform connection limits through three Bluetooth 5.1 channels and one wired USB-C interface.

The reason my Home Assistant ESP32s kept crashing isn't what you'd expect

It's important to know the limitations of your project boards

By  Joe Rice-Jones

The Clevetura felt like an ideal piece of kit

Being able to eliminate input device friction for my multi-machine workstation is a dream come true

The Clevetura S is built on a roughly 75% compact form factor, making it perfect for those who need extra space on their desk and don't want their keyboard to take up a massive footprint. What really sets the keyboard apart is TouchOnKeys technology, where each key features captive touch sensors embedded beneath the alphanumeric key grid.

Essentially, you can use the surface of your keyboard keys as a trackpad as well as a keyboard. Unlike some trackpads that rely solely on tap-to-click, the Clevetura S also includes two dedicated physical left- and right-click buttons positioned directly beneath the spacebar. On top of that, the top function row also incorporates captive touch sliders for volume, media scrubbing, or brightness adjustment, which you can program in the TouchOnKeys app.

Firmware dynamically distinguishes between vertical keystrokes and horizontal finger glides to prevent accidental cursor drift while you're typing. The board also uses low-profile scissor switches and flat ABS keys. Their closely spaced key profile is a functional necessity, allowing your fingers to track continuously across the touch matrix.

Clevetura provides the TouchOnKeys configuration utility across Windows, macOS, and Linux. This lets you enable firmware updates, adjust the Touchzone boundaries, and change sensitivity calibrations across all your operating systems.

item.itunes:title: 6 Android Auto settings Google hides but are actually worth turning on
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Connecting your phone to your car has improved in leaps and bounds with Android Auto, especially with the latest Coolwalk update, which brings a much-needed cosmetic refresh. That, along with several other improvements, has made this service my go-to when I need my phone's capabilities in my car. Helpfully, Google leaves immense scope for personalizing your user experience, but also hides several settings to keep the primary settings page simple and friendly.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Google hides most of these interesting settings under a secret menu called Developer Options, and it's separate from your device settings. Android Auto has its own settings meant for app devs, but enabling the menu is easy, and there's no reason to shy away from them if they improve system stability, convenience, or quality of life in a connected car.

Before we start, open Android Auto's menu under Settings > Connected devices > Connection preferences > Android Auto. Here, scroll to the bottom and tap the Version Number seven times quickly. You'll see a toast message confirming Developer Mode is enabled. You can access the settings on the same page by tapping the three-dot icon in the upper-right corner and selecting Developer settings. Contrary to popular belief, enabling this works independently of your Android system's Developer Options.

Ensure wireless connection stays out of the way

Or guarantees a stable connection

Android Auto is available on most cars as a wired or wireless connection. Years ago, you could toggle it on the main settings page to enable or disable wireless connection. With cordless convenience more common now, Google has moved this to the Developer settings section, but it remains available.

You should turn it on if you've been having issues with unstable wireless connections, and turning it off is also a good option if you're in the wired-connection camp. Several Android users report faster battery drain and connection instability when using adapters in vehicles that only support wired connections to begin with.

When you want to force a wired-only connection and sidestep all the pitfalls of the other options, you can turn off this toggle in Android Auto, so any wireless connection is summarily dismissed.

Have a razor-sharp screen

Custom scaling, but for your car

Android offers separate settings for the size of text, icons, and other elements on your phone. However, similar options aren't readily accessible on the main Android Auto settings page. This option, called Video Resolution in Developer options, is the key to fixing that, so you always have the sharpest screen.

By default, it's set to Allow Car and Phone to Negotiate, which means the car's display controller tells the phone its resolution. However, you can force supersampling by selecting a higher resolution than your display supports. The phone would send a higher-res signal, and the vehicle's controller would downsample it appropriately. Alternatively, you can force a suitable resolution if you're having trouble with instability over a wireless connection.

Finding the closest exact match to your display's native resolution can fix occasional issues with poorly optimized aftermarket headunits and odd-shaped displays where buttons and text may be way smaller or larger than desired. Matching the resolution ensures displays scale accurately, and important details like your vehicle position aren't occluded by your ETA in Google Maps' navigation view, for instance.

3 simple wireless Android Auto settings I changed on day one

I didn't expect to appreciate the convenience wireless Android Auto offers this much.

11
By  Patrick O'Rourke

Maximize your stereo's potential

One for the connoisseurs

While we're discussing video, it'd be remiss to skip the audio. I often write about how in-car audio is the closest thing you'd get to a home theater experience outside the home, isolated from the outside world with quality speakers placed around you. Now, whether you're using wired or wireless, there's a fair bit of processing happening before the sound goes from your phone to the car.

For the former, the audio is transmitted via USB protocol and sidesteps typical codecs to use uncompressed Pulse Code Modulation (PCM), but it may switch to the AAC codec if your car's headunit demands. On wireless, the car defaults to inferior, compressed audio codecs supported by the Bluetooth standard, such as AAC, SBC, or in some cases, Qualcomm's aptX.

You can use the developer settings to stay in control of in-car audio quality, so the vehicle and your phone don't default to the lowest common denominator. Select Audio codec in the menu and then pick the codec you want the phone to prefer — PCM, AAC-LC, or AAC-LC with ADTS headers. It should ensure you have the best possible audio quality at all times.

Disable app crash monitoring

Useful if you're familiar with your system's bugs

Android Auto has improved over the years, but much of that progress comes from crash reports and debugging when the software doesn't perform as intended. Android's bug report collection settings are independent and affect Auto, but if you're using a cheap wireless dongle or have frequent, momentary app freezes or crashes, the whole user experience can turn infuriating quickly.

By default, crash reporting shows you an error message on screen every time an app crashes. Android Auto's Developer Settings menu lets you turn off monitoring when an app becomes momentarily unresponsive. It works well when you find the unresponsiveness distracting or inconsequential. You just need to enable the Disable ANR Monitoring checkbox. Doing so lets devs continue debugging and using the UI even if a background app crashes.

Install apps from anywhere

Break free from the Play Store

We know the selection of apps compatible with Android Auto is barely a page long. However, that's just the Google Play Store, and if you're willing to expand your horizons and disregard some of Google's safety concerns, scores of independent developers are building FOSS apps for Android Auto, and some list their creations on alternative app stores.

Try downloading and installing them, and you'll notice they don't show up in your Android Auto app drawer at all. That's because there's one key toggle hidden in Developer Settings that Google reserves for devs. It allows you to install apps from unknown sources, such as beta builds in development that remain unsigned.

You can enable the checkbox beside Unknown Sources in the menu before sideloading apps from other sources. In our extensive experience, though, that's not a fix-all for problematic installations. We don't condone carefree sideloading, and the dev's guidance is often the best advice for successful installation, since the process and permissions needed for each app vary greatly. Importantly, this toggle will not make random apps on your phone Android Auto-ready. That requires the dedicated Android for Cars app library.

Fix your issues with wired Android Auto

Not starting? Here's the fix

This last option is hidden in your Android device settings, not the developer settings within the Android Auto page. By design, the main settings page for your in-car UI includes a toggle to start the Android Auto interface as soon as your vehicle connects to the car or a wireless adapter. It's called Start Android Auto automatically, but in some cases, the phone may connect to the car or adapter and Android Auto may not launch.

Typically, the culprit is how your phone handles a new USB connection. To change the default behavior that's causing the issue, connect your phone to your PC or car, then on the device, go to Settings > Connected devices > USB. Here, set the USB controlled by option to This device, and under Use USB for, choose File transfer, which is the same protocol used by Android Auto.

My old car's Android Auto stopped freezing after I lowered one hidden resolution setting

A resolute solution to the random crashes on dated systems.

By  Chandraveer Mathur

I should caution you that setting your phone up for file transfer by default poses a grave danger of juice-jacking if you frequently use public or shared charging cables. With the phone configured as above, we'd suggest using your own power brick or power bank instead of public amenities.

You have more control than you think

Android Auto doesn't bear all its settings in one place, but that doesn't mean that Google doesn't give you the controls. Those same options available to app devs might work wonders for your experience. Sometimes, they fix a months-long bother with a single toggle, or unlock new experiences with cool yet compatible apps not listed on the Play Store.

Or guarantees a stable connection

Android Auto is available on most cars as a wired or wireless connection. Years ago, you could toggle it on the main settings page to enable or disable wireless connection. With cordless convenience more common now, Google has moved this to the Developer settings section, but it remains available.

You should turn it on if you've been having issues with unstable wireless connections, and turning it off is also a good option if you're in the wired-connection camp. Several Android users report faster battery drain and connection instability when using adapters in vehicles that only support wired connections to begin with.

When you want to force a wired-only connection and sidestep all the pitfalls of the other options, you can turn off this toggle in Android Auto, so any wireless connection is summarily dismissed.

Have a razor-sharp screen

Custom scaling, but for your car

Android offers separate settings for the size of text, icons, and other elements on your phone. However, similar options aren't readily accessible on the main Android Auto settings page. This option, called Video Resolution in Developer options, is the key to fixing that, so you always have the sharpest screen.

By default, it's set to Allow Car and Phone to Negotiate, which means the car's display controller tells the phone its resolution. However, you can force supersampling by selecting a higher resolution than your display supports. The phone would send a higher-res signal, and the vehicle's controller would downsample it appropriately. Alternatively, you can force a suitable resolution if you're having trouble with instability over a wireless connection.

Finding the closest exact match to your display's native resolution can fix occasional issues with poorly optimized aftermarket headunits and odd-shaped displays where buttons and text may be way smaller or larger than desired. One for the connoisseurs

While we're discussing video, it'd be remiss to skip the audio. I often write about how in-car audio is the closest thing you'd get to a home theater experience outside the home, isolated from the outside world with quality speakers placed around you. Now, whether you're using wired or wireless, there's a fair bit of processing happening before the sound goes from your phone to the car.

For the former, the audio is transmitted via USB protocol and sidesteps typical codecs to use uncompressed Pulse Code Modulation (PCM), but it may switch to the AAC codec if your car's headunit demands. Useful if you're familiar with your system's bugs

Android Auto has improved over the years, but much of that progress comes from crash reports and debugging when the software doesn't perform as intended. Install apps from anywhere

Break free from the Play Store

We know the selection of apps compatible with Android Auto is barely a page long. Not starting? Here's the fix

Here, set the USB controlled by option to This device, and under Use USB for, choose File transfer, which is the same protocol used by Android Auto.

A resolute solution to the random crashes on dated systems.

I should caution you that setting your phone up for file transfer by default poses a grave danger of juice-jacking if you frequently use public or shared charging cables. With the phone configured as above, we'd suggest using your own power brick or power bank instead of public amenities.

You have more control than you think

Android Auto doesn't bear all its settings in one place, but that doesn't mean that Google doesn't give you the controls. Those same options available to app devs might work wonders for your experience. Sometimes, they fix a months-long bother with a single toggle, or unlock new experiences with cool yet compatible apps not listed on the Play Store.

item.title: Wake-on-LAN solved my NAS power problem, and it sleeps until I call it
item.itunes:title: Wake-on-LAN solved my NAS power problem, and it sleeps until I call it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
NAS, or Network Attached Storage, is a great way to build your own media storage, back up your precious memories or serve as a hub for your smart home automations. Whatever your use case, it is always a great idea to give it a break, especially if you are not doing something that requires the disks to keep spinning 24/7. The good news is that there is an easy way to set up your NAS to wake up when required and go to sleep when not in use.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

My NAS doesn’t need to be on all day

Most of the time, it’s waiting for me

My DS923+ does two jobs. It serves my media library through Plex, and it syncs media from my phone, serving as a backup. I use Plex in the evenings, and backups run when I need them. The rest of the day, nobody touches it. An always-on NAS makes sense for a business or a household that streams around the clock, but keeping mine running all day just for a few hours of real use felt wasteful.

The most obvious solution could be setting up drive hibernation. However, the issue is that drives rarely idle in a NAS. Synology has its own list of services that can stop drive hibernation, including DDNS, Plex, QuickConnect, and a host of other services. So, this wasn't a viable option for me, considering I have Plex running, not to mention my NAS connects to my desktop via SMB, which can also prevent drives from hibernating.

My home server goes to sleep when I don't need it, and instantly wakes up when I do

I decided to stop unnecessarily wasting electricity.

11
By  Rich Edmonds

Wake-on-LAN (WOL) fills the gap

It is helpful if you can't use hibernation and need additional control

Wake-on-LAN is an industry standard for network devices that lets you turn on or "wake up" a computer remotely as long as it is on the same network. It works by sending a special packet called a "magic packet" containing the target computer's MAC address over a UDP port. The target system, on the other hand, is usually in sleep mode with its NIC (Network Interface Card) active, so it can receive the packet over LAN and wake up the device.

Wake-on-LAN is a feature built into the NAS that can be used to power the device when needed. It has a few caveats, though. It only works after a proper shutdown (via the power button or the Shutdown option in DSM), and the power cord has to stay plugged in. It’s also only available on some models, and not on 10GbE ports.

You can fix the first issue using Synology's auto-power-off feature or, in my case, creating an auto-shutdown task. This is because auto power-off also relies on hibernation, which will not work if you have services like Plex running on the NAS. However, you can create a shutdown task to turn off the NAS every night when you go to bed, and wake it up in the morning using WOL when you need it.

Wake-on-LAN is the most useful home server feature nobody bothers to enable

Stop burning watts out of habit and start waking your server only when it has work to do.

By  Marshall Gunnell

To do this, you need to turn on WOL on your NAS, which you can do by following the steps below:

  1. On Synology DSM, open Control Panel -> Hardware & Power -> General.
  2. Under Power Recovery, tick Enable WOL on LAN 1 (and LAN 2 if you use a second port), then click Apply.
  3. DSM will also turn on Restart automatically when the power supply issue is fixed, which it requires for WOL.

Once done, you can move on to setting up a shutdown task on the NAS. Follow the steps below to set up the schedule:

  1. On your DSM, go to Control Panel -> Hardware & Power -> Power Schedule and click Create.
  2. Select Shutdown, choose the days and a time after you usually stop using the NAS, and click OK.
  3. Don’t create a startup task if you want the NAS to come back on only when you wake it.
I use Wake-on-LAN and a NAS to back up my PC even when I'm away from home
1
By  Rich Edmonds

The aforementioned steps will enable WOL and set up a nightly schedule. Next, you need to set up a way to send the magic packet to wake up the NAS. You can do so by installing Synology Assistant on your PC. When you launch the app, it searches and lists all the NAS devices that are connected to the network. You can then right-click on the NAS and choose WOL -> Wake Up. Similarly, you can download DS finder from the app store on your phone and set up WOL so that you can power your NAS using your phone as well. In both cases, your NAS should be powered on and connected to the same network in order to set up WOL.

The wait is the only trade-off

I'd rather wait for a few minutes if it means letting the NAS rest when not in use

The biggest drawback of WOL is that your NAS will take some time to wake up and be ready for use when you need it. However, for me, it is not a deal-breaker as the benefit of having it turned off when not in use outweighs the couple of minutes that I need to wait for it to power on. Also, over time, I have gotten used to it and usually use the DS finder app to turn on the NAS when I need to stream something or back up my media files. So the NAS doesn't run around the clock, but it's ready for me when I needit.

My NAS runs on my schedule now

Let it rest until you need it

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

My DS923+ rests when not in use and wakes up when I need to access its data. This keeps the drives from working and running around the clock. And of course, not having the drives spin all the time helps extend the lifespan of my hard drives as well.

WOL is a great tool that ensures the device is not idling all day just for me to watch a movie or TV show late at night after work. This may not work for some, especially those who run automation or other services that require the device to be active 24/7. However, if you are one of those who don't need NAS all the time, then WOL might just be the best option for you.

item.title: I gave my local LLM one job that runs every morning, and it's done more for me than a year of chatting with it
item.itunes:title: I gave my local LLM one job that runs every morning, and it's done more for me than a year of chatting with it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've spent an embarrassing amount of time testing local LLMs, only to discover that most of them make pretty terrible chatbots. They're slow, confidently wrong about basic things, and often need several prompts to complete a task that ChatGPT handles in one. Running AI on your own hardware is cool, but the novelty wears off quickly when you have to babysit every response.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I've started to think automations are a far better use for these smaller models. Give one a specific job, supply the information it needs, and let it run in the background without expecting it to be a general-purpose assistant. That's what I did with a morning briefing that goes through my emails, messages, tasks, notes, and work dashboards, then tells me what deserves my attention that day. It's easily the most useful thing I've done with a local LLM.

I turned my local LLM into a morning assistant

One job, every single morning

I've been using n8n for automations for quite some time, so that's where I started. I built a workflow that runs every morning and collects information scattered across the apps I use for work. This includes emails, Slack messages, tasks in Asana, calendar events, notes, and data from internal dashboards. JBL Vibe Beam

JBL Vibe Beam wireless earbuds are inexpensive, charge quickly, and have an eight-hour battery life.

See at Amazon

Why the JBL Vibe Beam are still worth it at this price

If you've been looking for a dependable set of true wireless buds to toss in a pocket or a bag, this is the one to grab. The 8mm drivers in the Vibe Beam are tuned for JBL Deep Bass Sound, which means the low-end hits noticeably harder than what you'd get from a generic $25 pair of buds.

The stick-closed design seals out external noise passively, and that seal is what makes the bass feel tight instead of muddy. It's not active noise cancelling, but for the price, the sound isolation is more than enough for commuting, workouts, or just blocking out an open office.

TalkThru lets you pause and hear people around you without pulling the buds out, and Ambient Aware keeps the music playing while letting in outside sound.

VoiceAware adjusts how much of your own voice you hear during hands-free calls, which makes stereo calls sound more natural than the typical single-mic budget earbuds.

Grab them at $29.95 on Amazon while the price holds. It's the lowest they've been in 30 days, and for a pair of earbuds that sound this good and last this long, it's an easy call.

item.title: I got my RTX 4090 under 300W without tanking my 1% lows, and the power limit slider wasn’t enough
item.itunes:title: I got my RTX 4090 under 300W without tanking my 1% lows, and the power limit slider wasn’t enough
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If you already know the basics of undervolting, I won't bore you with another generic tuning tutorial. What rarely gets talked about is the hilarious paradox of the flagship GPU silicon. At one point, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's infamous ​​​​​​"The more you buy, the more you save" catchphrase becomes true, at least on your power bill. While my 2022 Zotac RTX 4090 Trinity OC carries a 450W power rating on the box, taming it with MSI Afterburner unlocked a much lower power draw and consistent performance once I got past the usual stability shenanigans that come bundled with every undervolt.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

With hardware this powerful, I no longer chase FPS. Even in 2026, a card like the RTX 4090 has more than enough horsepower to deliver high frame rates, provided the games are properly optimized. Between upscaling and frame generation, hitting big FPS numbers is rarely a problem anymore. At first, I took the easy route and dragged the power limit slider down, forcing the GPU to stay below 270W. However, I wasn't satisfied with the GPU's behavior and overall gameplay performance. Only then did I decide to lock the voltage curve instead. And through some experimentation, I discovered just how efficient the RTX 4090 can be.

The surprising reason I finally undervolted my GPU

It wasn't the temps or the coil whine

1
By  Tanveer Singh

Why the no-frills power limit slider changes GPU clock behavior and tanks 1% lows

Choking board power down to 60% drops clock speeds without delivering true efficiency

My real concern is longevity, and I've been skeptical ever since I bought the card. My 12VHPWR connector hasn't melted yet, but watching the power consumption creep toward 400W under heavy synthetic loads has always made me uneasy. For most, the power slider is the go-to shortcut. On both AMD and Nvidia GPUs, you can lower the cap in your vendor's OEM software or Afterburner with a single click.

However, as soon as you launch a demanding game at 4K with a 60% power slider, Nvidia's GPU Boost algorithm lowers the default clocks in real time based on available power, severely crippling my GPU's efficiency potential. In my case, the entire test session felt sluggish and, more importantly, the 1% lows were inconsistent and kept dipping between 45–50FPS; GPU clocks remained inconsistent between 2,350MHz and 2,400MHz, and it still pulled more power than my undervolt while running at lower clocks.

At 1440p, with the 60% power slider on, my 4090 pulled 270W at just 2,300MHz, and at either resolution, 1440p or 4K, the gameplay had micro-stuttering, leaving me dissatisfied with the results.

How my tuned RTX 4090 dropped below 250W while keeping clocks stable

Testing real-world silicon efficiency in Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced at 4K and 1440p

Undervolting takes more patience on the RTX 40 series because its boost behavior scales, so it took me a while to dial in a stable profile across multiple gaming sessions and synthetic tests such as FurMark and OCCT stability tests. Even at stock settings in Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced, my 4090 stays well shy of its 450W TDP, peaking at 365W at 1.050V and averaging around 320-350W at 4K. Temperatures were never a problem because Zotac's cooler never let the GPU core temperature cross 72℃, the memory above 80℃, and the hotspot above 90℃, whether the GPU is stock or undervolted.

For my in-game settings, I ran Raytracing Mode set to Extended and BVH Quality on High, paired with 75% custom DLSS resolution scaling using DLSS 4.0 (310.6), and Preset K to balance image quality and frame rate. Frame Generation was disabled entirely, as shown in the frame-time graph in my screenshots. At 4K with that 75% custom scaling, my stock setup averaged 66FPS with 1% lows sitting at 58FPS.

Once I applied the V/F curve shown in the screenshots above and locked the core to 2,550MHz at 0.93V, my 365W peak at 4K dropped to 250W-253W territory. Average performance dipped by roughly 5% to 63FPS, with 1% lows at 53FPS. Since the core clock remained pinned at 2,550MHz and didn't dip below 2,400MHz as it did with the slider, gameplay felt much smoother, and the 1% lows stopped dropping. Intrigued, I tested the same game settings at 1440p, where it showed an even wider efficiency gap: peak wattage sat at 210–220W and dropped as low as 186W while standing near the ocean, beating the 1440p 60% slider's 270W consumption while running 250MHz faster.

Those 1440p power draw figures sit only slightly above an RTX 5060 or RTX 5060 Ti at stock settings, showing how much efficiency is hiding inside the flagship die when you stop feeding it excess voltage. For all of these runs, I stayed on the 610.88 WHQL driver, which has remained stable across my testing and avoids the washed-out HDR contrast bug that popped up in later driver releases.

Shouldn't a flagship GPU always be pushed to its maximum limit?

Trading a 5% frame difference for over 100W less heat and connector stress makes sense

Many enthusiasts argue that when paying for an expensive flagship GPU, holding back its clock ceiling makes little sense, and they aren't wrong. Some go a step further by cross-flashing another vendor's 600W vBIOS to squeeze every last frame out of the die. Still, the raw performance of the stock RTX 4090, especially in well-optimized games, leaves plenty of headroom. In my case, I traded in more than 100W of heat for roughly a 5% frame difference, but I achieved my objective: lower power draw and stable 1% lows that translate to smoother gameplay.

A smarter voltage curve can make your GPU last longer

Ultimately, these test results are specific to my setup and limited to my GPU only. As with CPUs, your undervolting mileage will vary due to the silicon lottery and other factors. Even so, relying on factory voltage curves or simply dragging the power slider leaves real efficiency gains on the table. Spending a little time figuring out what works best for your GPU is well worth the effort, especially when it trims your power bill and keeps an expensive GPU and its power cable running cooler under load.

item.title: I ran Qwen3.8 with its censorship trained out, and it stopped overthinking
item.itunes:title: I ran Qwen3.8 with its censorship trained out, and it stopped overthinking
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Local models have come a long way over the past year, and there's just no denying that they are far more capable and trustworthy than they were ever before. In the discourse surrounding local AI, users often obsess over details like a model's size, parameters, how many tokens per second it pushes, and where it lands on the leaderboard. Those numbers tell you how well a model runs, but not what it learned. So, does it matter how a model is trained? It does once you trust its responses, because a biased response can steer you the wrong way quite easily.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

According to Nous Research, Qwen3.8-27B refuses, deflects, or repeats the Chinese government's framing on politically sensitive subjects, and its version of the fix is Arete-27B. However, every retrain risks breaking something else, so I ran both models on my RTX 4070 Ti Super with an everyday question, and then, the same question with web search capabilities to find out.

What is Arete-27B?

It's Qwen3.8 with one key distinguisher

Nous Research, the lab behind Hermes Agent, released Arete-27B earlier in November. The model is Qwen3.8-27B with a supervised fine-tune on top, trained on answers from Inkling, the open model from Thinking Machines Lab, across seven politically touchy areas, from free expression to surveillance. The lab says that, in their testing, propaganda-laced answers to specific questions asked to the model fell from 22% to 0.9% in its 803-prompt test.

It's worth noting that it's different from the abliterated, "uncensored" Qwen3.8 builds you'd normally find on Hugging Face, which rip out refusals across the board. Arete-27B is a targeted retrain, and Nous says that it lost next to nothing in the retraining process, scoring 65.60% on its Hermes Bench against the original's 65.77%. It comes under the Apache 2.0 license, and the training data as well as the test set are public as well.

I ran both the models in llama-server on my RTX 4070 Ti Super, alongside a Ryzen 5 7600X and 32GB of DDR5-6000 memory. The default Q4_K_M files won't fit in the 16GB of GDDR6X my GPU has, so I used bartowski's IQ4_XS quants, at 15.2GB and 15.5GB respectively, leaving about 2GB for everything else. Both the models ran with the thinking-mode samplers from Qwen's model card, with temperature at 1.0, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, and min_p at 0.

I tested every tiny local LLM worth running, and only three survived the cut

Small models are doing more than they should

1
By  Nolen Jonker

I asked both models to choose between a Xiaomi and a Pixel

Both picked the Pixel, but Arete got there with far less thinking

The most obvious place to start was the one thing Nous says it changed, or rather, fine-tuned, which is how the model answers queries relating to its bias. Instead of just re-running Nous's own tests, I went with an everyday question that a user is likely to ask the model, and also the one where invisible bias could contribute to flawed decision-making. I gave both models the exact same prompt:

"I'm deciding between a Xiaomi phone and a Google Pixel for my next phone, and privacy matters to me. What personal data does each company collect, where does it end up, and who could get access to it? Then tell me which one you'd pick for someone like me."

Surprisingly enough, both the models leaned towards the Pixel, but in their reasoning, weighed the two governments differently. Arete called Chinese state access a structural risk that Google has no real equivalent for, while Qwen spent more time on US surveillance, and warned that a Pixel wouldn't do much for me if that was my main worry.

Neither model, however, nailed the facts. Qwen listed most of the regions where Xiaomi says it stores data, while Arete stopped at "China and/or other countries." Qwen talked about a "permissionless location" setting that Google's own Pixel pages don't mention, and Arete mixed up two different Pixel privacy features. There were also differences in how long each model thought. Arete reasoned for 3,371 words, whereas Qwen took about 6,000 to reach its verdict.

I dropped Qwen and Gemma for a 27B model that runs smoothly on my 8GB graphics card

Chasing a big number finally paid off

10
By  Nolen Jonker

Web search made Arete quicker and Qwen more careful

Qwen needed double the context to get there

For the last test, I connected both models to the SearXNG instance I set up, and sent the same Xiaomi and Pixel prompt with one extra line asking them to search the web and cite their sources. Both of the models started with the same samplers and 32K of context.

Arete was efficient and quick, which was remarkable for a model based on Qwen3.8. It ran nine searches, read four pages, and surprisingly enough, set a character limit on every page it pulled in. It wrapped up in about 15 minutes, using about 22K tokens of context.

Qwen3.8, on the other hand, kept running out of context at 32K. I had to double it to 64K with an 8-bit cache before it finished, and it took 38 minutes across 12 searches, and 12 page reads, with not a single one of them being capped. A good chunk of that went into chasing a Romanian fine against Xiaomi and a 404 Media story it half-remembered and never found.

I'd be lying if I said the extra effort didn't show up in the answer, though. Qwen read through Xiaomi's privacy policy, told me which sites blocked it, and dropped the claims it couldn't confirm.

Arete took a study of phones sold in China and applied it to every Xiaomi, cited a figure from a page it never really managed to read, and leaned on a forum post. Qwen's performance wasn't spotless either, since it overstated what U.S. national security letters can pull from Google. Both models still picked the Pixel. However, both sounded more certain than they did without search.

Arete-27B is the easier model to live with on a 16GB card

Over one run of each test, Arete-27B thought less, searched less, and finished within 32K context, while Qwen needed double the context and a lot more time in the same test. What Arete didn't do, though, was to check its sources as meticulously as Qwen did. If I were using it for research today, I'd run Arete for everyday questions, but still double-check anything it finds online.

item.title: KDE’s brand-new Ghostty-based terminal has been released, and it’s GPU-accelerated
item.itunes:title: KDE’s brand-new Ghostty-based terminal has been released, and it’s GPU-accelerated
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Kwi v0.1 has been released, and is no longer just experimental; still a work-in-progress with some bugs and missing bits.
  • New tweaks from the original build include Shift+Up/Down scrolling and improved link detection.
  • You can download the nightly build right now, and a Flatpak version is currently under review.

A little while ago, KDE announced the existence of Kwi. It's a new terminal aimed at bringing the technology up to speed with modern protocols, and it will make it easier for developers to integrate it into their apps. At the time, KDE said that Kwi wasn't even at v0.1 and was highly experimental.

Now, KDE has revealed that Kwi is no longer just an experiment, and has taken the very first step toward becoming a stable app. You can now try Kwi v0.1, and there have been some nice new additions since its first release.

Kwi v0.1 is now ready to download

A Flatpak is on the way, too

As announced on the KDE website, Kwi is ready to download right now. It's an official v0.1 release, so it's not quite in the experimental state we saw a few weeks ago, but it's still very much a work in progress. As such, expect missing bits, bugs, and some translation issues as the KDE community fleshes it out.

Since its reveal, Kwi has gone through the KDE review system and is now recognized as a KDE project. You can also hide the tab bar when you have only a single tab open, and you can finally scroll using the Shift + Up or Down arrow keys. There are a bunch of other tweaks we've listed in the expandable box below, so if you gave Kwi a try in the past and found it lacking, now's a good time to see if your pet peeves got fixed.

KDE has submitted Kwi to Flathub, and at the time of writing, it's still under review. If you can't wait, you can either download the files if you're a distro manager, or check out the README for instructions on how to grab the nightly build if you just want to give it a spin.

As promised, here are the full notes of improvements since Kwi launched:

Progress Tracker

  • Terminal:
    • Link hover decorations are now always shown; opening a link still requires pressing the Ctrl key, unless you change the setting for this (feedback on Matrix)
    • Link detection is more robust, avoiding certain false positives (bug #528844)

  • General UI:
    • Support for global menus and the menu button on the window title bar has landed
    • Tapping Kwi on touchscreens will now open the on-screen keyboard (user request on Matrix)

  • Tab bar:
    • The much-requested option to hide the tab bar for single tabs has materialized (work item #6)
    • Tab traversal using Ctrl+Tab now follows last-used order instead of just going between the last two active tabs (feature request #528798)
    • The minimum width of tab buttons has been reduced considerably, allowing more tabs to fit before the tab bar scrolls (user request on Matrix)
    • Kwi no longer forgets to select the last remaining tab when all others have been closed

  • Theming:
    • It's now possible to select the system color scheme that Kwi windows should use (separately from the terminal color scheme) (popular request)
